body.p: Applicant respectfully traverses the Notice of Non-Compliant Amendment on the grounds that it is improper.

First of all, it is a fundamental principle of the examination process that, after every amendment, the Examiner must reevaluate the patentability of the claims in light of the amendments, including establishing a broadest reasonable interpretation of the claims and comparing that interpretation to the previous rejection rationale to see if it is still applicable. It is a troubling symptom of the Office's policy on double patenting rejections in continuations that the Examiner would apparently consider it self-evident that a double patenting rejection would still have to be addressed even after Applicant substantially amended the independent claims and introduced a new independent claim that has never even been rejected for double patenting. Applicant's response was fully compliant - the previous rejections became moot upon filing and the burden has now shifted to the Examiner to determine whether double-patenting applies to the amended/new claims.
Moreover, the Examiner has already determined that double-patenting does not apply to the claims that supported the amended/new claims. The Examiner stated:
Claims 21-23 and 31-33 are rejected on the ground of nonstatutory double patenting as being
unpatentable over claims 1-8, 12-17 of U.S. Patent No. 11399777. Although the claims at issue are not
identical, they are not patentably distinct from each other because US 11399777 B2 claims: Office A ction at page 6. And:
Claims 24, 30, 34 and 40 are objected to as being dependent upon a rejected base claim, but
would be allowable if rewritten in independent form including all of the limitations of the base claim and
any intervening claims.
Office A ction at page 7. Accordingly, it is a matter of record that claims 24, 30, 34, and 40 are free of double patenting. The undersigned stated:
Applicant thanks the Examiner for the indication of allowable subject matter. While Applicant has
not included the limitations of claims 30 and 40 in the respective independent claims 21 and 31 verbatim,

Applicant has used the insight in crafting the present amendments. Applicant also has added new claim 41 which is intended to be the allowable claim 24 in independent form. Claim 42 recites the same limitation as
claim 23.
Applicant's Response dated Aug. 22, 2024 at page 5. At the time of filing the response, it was impossible that any double patenting issues were outstanding and therefore the Notice of
Non-Compliant Amendment was improper.
Applicants are not required to argue in favor of patentability, nor to conjecture about potential

rejections that an Examiner may make in the future. The fact that the Examiner seems to place emphasis on the fact that Applicant departed from rewriting the claims verbatim only highlights the point that the ball is now in the Examiner's court to analyze the amended/new claims.

If the Examiner now believes that the wording differences from allowable Claim 30 to amended Claim 21 are so different that double patenting arises, the appropriate course of action according to Office policy is to analyze the claims and offer a rationale for rejection in a Final Rejection (e.g., provide prima facie evidence of double patenting). That said, the undersigned had, and still has, every reason to believe that the amended claim 21 (right column (formatted to aid in comparison)) is allowable based on the Examiner's own former finding (left column):
Similarly, it seems extremely unlikely that double patenting applies to Claim 41 based on the previous analysis.
Applicant maintains that the claims are in condition for allowance.
